text: You're given a 2D grid of ones, which are land, and zeros, which are water. An island is land connected up, down, left, or right. Return the number of islands.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — connectivity is four-directional only, not diagonal, and an island can be any number of connected land cells. So I'm really counting connected components of land. Is that right?

One detail I want to note early — the grid holds characters, the character one and the character zero, not integers. I'll keep the quotes in mind when I compare and write cells. And can I modify the grid in place, or should I treat it as read-only?

Let me run through the example. Take this small grid — a pair of land cells at the top left, a vertical pair on the right, and a single cell at the bottom left. That's three separate land groups, so the answer is three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to reach for Union-Find, unioning adjacent land cells and counting distinct roots. That works, but it's more machinery than needed here. This problem reminds me of flood fill. I scan the grid; each time I hit land I haven't seen, that's a new island — I count it and sink the whole connected piece with DFS so I don't count it again. Simple and linear.

Here's the plan. One: scan every cell. Two: when a cell is land, add one to the count and launch a DFS from it. Three: the DFS returns on out-of-bounds or water; otherwise it sinks the cell to zero and recurses into its four neighbors. So the grid itself is my visited marker. One thing worth flagging — I sink the current cell before I recurse. If I recursed first, two adjacent cells would call each other forever, A into B and B back into A while A is still land, and blow the stack. There's a trade-off here. Sinking mutates the input, and on a huge all-land grid the recursion can get m times n deep and overflow — so for very large inputs I'd switch to BFS with a queue. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Two nested loops scan the grid; each unseen land cell bumps the count and starts a DFS. The DFS checks bounds and water first, sinks the cell, then visits four neighbors from a small directions table. One thing worth flagging — the comparisons use the characters one and zero, with quotes. The grid is char, so a bare one in the scan compares against character code one, never matches, and the function silently returns zero. The same slip in the DFS base case is worse: a sunk cell no longer stops the recursion, so neighbors bounce back and forth until the stack overflows.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. The same grid, expected output three. The moment that matters is right after the first launch: at row zero, column zero, the count goes to one and DFS sinks the whole top-left pair, so when the scan reaches the next cell it sees water and skips it. The right-hand pair works the same way. Three launches, so it returns three. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. An all-water grid returns zero — no DFS ever launches. A single land cell returns one. A grid that's entirely land also returns one — one DFS sinks everything.

The time complexity is m times n — each cell is scanned once and sunk at most once. The space complexity is also m times n, for the recursion stack in the worst case. In the worst-case scenario, one snake-shaped island filling the grid makes the stack that deep. Oh, one more thing — that deep-stack case is exactly when I'd reach for BFS instead. A queue keeps the frontier on the heap and won't overflow the call stack. Same time.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as counting connected components, with the count equal to DFS launches. You caught the char-versus-int trap and flagged that sinking must happen before recursing or the stack blows. And you noted the destructive-input and deep-recursion trade-offs, with BFS as the fix. Good work.
